_about: The words of the full Letters to the Nations that tools/build_letters.py writes (wave 1 of the full blueprints, 25 November 2026). For each nation: what it has already built (one paragraph, every figure from a line on its blueprint) and the sources of that paragraph. The opening, the quotation and the seal come from tools/nation/<slug>.json; the work ahead from data/<slug>.json.

algeria.built: Look at what you are already building. In January 2026 your Treasury opened its first sovereign sukuk, drawing on national savings for roads, equipment and public services, and by April more than four-fifths had been subscribed. The African Development Bank is financing the 495-kilometre railway from Laghouat to El Meniaa, and at Adrar, in the south, a US$3.5 billion dairy farm and powdered-milk plant is rising to feed the nation from its own land.

benin.built: Look at what you are already building. In January 2026 you sold your first international sukuk, US$500 million over seven years, and in September a guarantee from the African Development Fund helped you raise €500 million from international banks for twelve years, for schools, clinics, water and power. In Cotonou and its neighbours, US$400 million from the World Bank is building safer and faster roads along the corridors where most of your jobs are.

burkina-faso.built: Look at what you are already building. In 2026 your own people, at home and abroad, lent you XOF 151.5 billion through the Diaspora Bonds, well above the XOF 125 billion you sought. In March 2026 alone the West African Development Bank approved XOF 131.5 billion for you: inputs for the cotton farmers, a larger solar plant with batteries at Koudougou, and the fuel that keeps the country moving.

cabo-verde.built: Look at what you are already building. The wind of Santiago turns the turbines of Cabeólica, your first independent power producer, which already makes about a fifth of your electricity, and new turbines and batteries came on line in December 2025. The European Investment Bank and the European Union are rebuilding your ports with €147 million, and the World Bank Group has committed US$1.08 billion across 56 projects to an island nation of half a million people.

cameroon.built: Look at what you are already building. In 2026 the African Development Bank approved €309.9 million to pave the road that opens up the East and €81.2 million for hillside dams that bring water to the farms of the North, and the World Bank launched a US$1.12 billion programme to modernise the corridor from the port of Douala to Bangui. In January you returned to the international market and raised US$750 million.

central-african-republic.built: Look at what you are already building. In August 2026 the Sakaï 2 solar field at Bimbo began to feed the grid of Bangui, and the World Bank Group now counts 76 projects in your country, worth US$3.15 billion. In June 2026 it approved the first phase of a US$1.12 billion programme for the corridor that links Bangui to the sea at Douala.

chad.built: Look at what you are already building. In July 2025 the IMF approved a four-year programme of about US$625 million, and in August 2026 Afreximbank signed its largest financing ever for Chad. Across your 23 provinces, 145,000 families have already bought solar kits through a World Bank project, and new financing is building roads to your markets and your neighbours.

gabon.built: Look at what you are already building. In 2023 you refinanced US$500 million of your bonds to protect your ocean, the first such debt conversion for marine conservation in mainland Africa. In 2026 the markets lent you US$920 million and then US$580 million, and the World Bank is bringing piped water, electricity and safe sanitation to more homes with US$150 million.

gambia.built: Look at what you are already building. The European Investment Bank has signed €105.5 million for solar power with batteries on your grid, and for solar units at rural clinics, schools and food stores. In June 2026 the World Bank approved US$50 million to bring reliable, clean electricity to more Gambian homes, and in September BADEA signed a US$100 million facility so the food and fuel the nation needs keep arriving.

guinea.built: Look at what you are already building. In December 2025 the first iron ore from Simandou left your shores, carried by a new railway to a new port, with the nation holding 15% of the line. In June 2026 the World Bank Group endorsed a partnership of more than US$3 billion to 2033 and approved, on a single day, US$116 million for commercial farming, US$102 million for skills and US$75 million for public finances.

liberia.built: Look at what you are already building. In April 2026 the IMF approved about US$266 million to help you build buffers against climate shocks, and the World Bank and its partners are bringing solar power, broadband and roads to the south-east. In November 2026 a new project began to support communities that keep your forests standing, with a goal of 50,000 jobs.

libya.built: Look at what you are already building. In April 2026 your two chambers agreed the first unified state budget since 2013, about US$30 billion, a step the World Bank calls a landmark for fiscal discipline. In January you signed a 25-year agreement for the Waha fields that brings more than US$20 billion of foreign investment, and in June US$3.26 billion of oil revenue reached the sovereign account.

mali.built: Look at what you are already building. In June 2026 investors across the region lent you XOF 55 billion, and then XOF 55 billion again. The West African Development Bank is financing a 50-megawatt solar plant with batteries at Tiètiguila and the harvest of your cotton, and the African Development Bank, the Islamic Development Bank and BOAD are building a 225 kV loop that raises the power reaching Bamako to 600 megawatts.

mauritania.built: Look at what you are already building. You have brought your public debt down from 52.4% of GDP in 2021 to 39.9% in 2025, and in June 2026 the IMF approved a new 42-month programme. The World Bank is financing a US$465 million power corridor that ties you into the West African electricity market, so the wind and sun of your coast can light your neighbours too.

mauritius.built: Look at what you are already building. You hold US$10.3 billion of reserves, and your law now anchors public debt at 75% of GDP by June 2030. Four new solar plants with batteries, financed by your own banks, will supply 8% of the nation’s electricity, and India is financing a new national hospital, a motorway and a new control tower with US$655 million.

niger.built: Look at what you are already building. Your crude now flows by pipeline to the coast of Benin, and in May 2026 you cut the cost of that journey from US$27 to US$15 a barrel. The World Bank finances 23 operations worth US$4.6 billion in your country, among them the Kandadji dam, and in April 2026 the African Development Bank approved US$180.6 million for young farmers in all eight regions.

sierra-leone.built: Look at what you are already building. In 2024 you signed a US$480 million compact with the Millennium Challenge Corporation to carry power to schools, clinics, businesses and homes, and in June 2026 the IMF approved US$211.5 million to build resilience to climate shocks. The OPEC Fund is financing 60 more megawatts of clean power at Bumbuna for Freetown.

sudan.built: Even in war, you have kept working. The Kenana sugar factory never stopped, families still receive salaries and help through a mobile banking app, and engineers have brought piped water back to Port Sudan. Partners stand with you: in April 2026 the African Development Bank approved US$87 million to help your farmers grow more food.

togo.built: Look at what you are already building. In June 2026 the World Bank approved US$200 million to modernise your transport and logistics around the Port of Lomé, and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank joined it with US$75 million. In 2025 the World Bank and IFC launched a US$300 million programme to make you a regional hub for agribusiness and animal feed.

tunisia.built: Look at what you are already building. You have repaid your debts on time and you finance most of your needs at home. In June 2026 you negotiated a US$500 million loan from Afreximbank, and brought its rate down from 9% to 5.86%.
